Tokyo Electron stock gets stronger fiscal 2027 outlook
sum: Tokyo Electron reported stronger first-half results for fiscal 2027 on October 30, as investment linked to AI servers and data centers supported demand for semiconductor production equipment. Investing.com, citing a Reuters report, said the company also issued its first full-year forecast and approved a share repurchase program.

Revenue for the six months ended September rose 41.3 percent to 1.67 trillion yen. Operating income increased 67.2 percent to 506.78 billion yen, while net income attributable to shareholders climbed 56 percent to 376.93 billion yen.

The first-half performance exceeded Tokyo Electron's earlier targets. Revenue was 2.9 percent above the previous estimate, operating income beat the plan by 10.6 percent and attributable net income came in 8 percent above the earlier forecast, according to the Investing.com report.

Tokyo Electron's first full-year forecast covers the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027. The company expects revenue of 3.7 trillion yen, operating income of 1.169 trillion yen and attributable net income of 865 billion yen.

The outlook reflects expanding demand for AI servers and higher customer investment in semiconductor manufacturing equipment. It also shifts the focus to execution in the second half, when the company must convert elevated customer spending into deliveries and earnings.

For investors, the forecast provides a clearer framework for assessing the stock after the strong first half. The key issue is whether demand for equipment used in advanced semiconductor production remains strong enough to support the new targets through March.

The board approved a share repurchase program of up to 150 billion yen. Purchases are scheduled to run from November 1, 2026, through March 31, 2027. The authorization covers the period in which the company will report its second-half progress, but the approved ceiling does not by itself guarantee that the full amount will be used.

Nikkei Stock Average Falls for First Time in Four Days as Nvidia CEO Dismissal Report Sparks Selling in AI, Semiconductor Shares
sum: On Nov. 12, the Nikkei Stock Average fell for the first time in four trading days on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, closing at 60,819.36, down 429.23 yen (0.70%) from the previous session. Following a report that the board of U.S. semiconductor giant Nvidia is preparing to dismiss CEO Jensen Huang, selling spread across AI and semiconductor-related shares. The market had opened higher in the morning, lifted by a tech rally in the previous day's U.S. session, but selling gained the upper hand in the afternoon.

The TOPIX rose 7.94 points (0.20%) to 3,937.33, extending its winning streak to four sessions, while the TSE Prime Market Index was up 0.21% at 2,029.52. Trading value on the Prime Market reached ¥9.0867 trillion (approximately $56.8 billion). Among the TSE's 33 sector indexes, 27 sectors advanced, including fisheries and agriculture, rubber, and food products, while six sectors declined, including services, nonferrous metals, and electric appliances. On the Prime Market, 959 issues (61%) advanced, 548 (35%) declined and 44 (2%) were unchanged, with advancers accounting for about 60% of all issues despite the index's decline.

Regarding Huang, U.S. authorities are reportedly investigating suspicions that he leaked information to China through a woman with whom he had an extramarital affair, and reports said the company's board would decide to dismiss him. With uncertainty over a successor to the charismatic leader, risk-off sentiment spread, and Advantest (6857.T) and Ibiden (4062.T), both seen as major suppliers to Nvidia, were sold from the morning session. In the afternoon, other AI-related stocks including Tokyo Electron (8035.T) and SoftBank Group (9984.T) trimmed gains or turned negative, weighing on the index.
The Nikkei rose as much as 539.85 yen to 61,788.44 at 11:19 a.m. before turning lower in the afternoon session, at one point falling 604.80 yen to 60,643.79 at 2:46 p.m.
Note: The TSE Growth Market 250 Index fell for the first time in four days.

In other Asian markets, South Korea's KOSPI, which is heavily dependent on the semiconductor sector, fell 0.6%, and the Taiwan Weighted Index dropped 2.6%, while U.S. Nasdaq futures were also soft in after-hours trading. Intermittent selling in Nikkei futures also weighed on the index.

sum: In the morning session of the Tokyo stock market on the 11th, the Nikkei Stock Average extended its gains, closing the morning at 60,942.48, up 482.90 points (0.80%) from the previous day. Bargain-hunting sentiment created by the sharp drop following the U.S. midterm elections, combined with improved supply-demand conditions from the unwinding of margin buying positions, drew buying from individual investors with ample funds, pushing the market higher. In early trading, the market briefly turned negative on the previous day's U.S. stock declines and SoftBank Group's (SBG) drop, but recovered after selling ran its course, with the gain at one point expanding to nearly 800 points.

The Tokyo Stock Price Index (TOPIX) also extended gains, closing the morning at 3,924.51, up 30.80 points (0.79%) from the previous day. The JPX Prime 150 Index also ended the morning session higher. At the morning close, trading value on the Tokyo Stock Exchange's Prime Market was approximately ¥4.0929 trillion (approximately $25.8 billion), with volume at 1.199 billion shares. Advancing issues numbered 914, accounting for nearly 60% of the total, while decliners totaled 593 and unchanged issues 44.

Semiconductor-related shares drove the market higher. Buying flowed into Advantest, Tokyo Electron, Lasertec, TDK, Ibiden, and Taiyo Yuden. Last week, the Nikkei plunged below 60,000 on selling of artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor stocks following the U.S. midterm election results, with the decline accelerating as individual investors trading on margin sold at a loss. Margin buying positions have since decreased somewhat, lightening supply-demand conditions and creating an environment conducive to buybacks. Kioxia, whose margin buying positions appear to be unwinding, also rose.

After buying flowed first into domestic-demand stocks with strong earnings and undervalued shares such as banks, brokerages, and trading houses, the buying spread to semiconductor stocks. In step with the rise in South Korea's KOSPI, buying of stock index futures—apparently by overseas short-term traders—intensified, and the Nikkei briefly climbed above 61,000.

sum: On Nov. 9, the Nikkei Stock Average rebounded for the first time in six sessions on the Tokyo stock market, closing at 58,775.50, up 1,340.73 points (2.33%) from the end of the previous week. Carrying over the buyback of high-tech and semiconductor-related stocks in the U.S. market late last week, buying in Tokyo also led with a broad range of issues, centering on artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor-related names. However, after buying ran its course, selling on rebounds capped the upside, and many see the move as within the scope of a technical rebound.

The Nikkei opened at 57,960.70, up 525.93 points, and the advance briefly exceeded 2,000 points to reach 59,440. After ending morning trading at 59,411.34, up 1,976.57 points (3.44%) from the end of the previous week, the index trimmed its gains in the afternoon. On the Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market, advancing issues totaled 1,415 (91%), amounting to gains across nearly the entire market, while decliners were limited to 123 issues (7%). Trading value was ¥8.911842 trillion (approximately $56.4 billion), and volume was 2.99581 billion shares.

On the Tokyo market on Friday, Nov. 6, stocks fell across the board amid concerns over a slowdown in AI-related investment and tighter data center regulations after Democrats won the U.S. midterm elections, with the Nikkei's decline exceeding 3,600 points — the third-largest closing drop on record. The rebound on Nov. 9 was a reaction to that selloff.

By sector, 31 of the 33 Tokyo Stock Exchange sectors rose, with only foods and marine transportation declining. The top gainers by percentage included nonferrous metals, banking, other products, oil and coal products, and electric appliances. Among individual stocks, high-priced AI-related names such as Tokyo Electron (8035.T) and Advantest (6857.T) were bought, and Fast Retailing (9983.T) was the top positive contributor to the Nikkei. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (7011.T), Furukawa Electric (5801.T), and Minebea Mitsumi (6479.T) were also firm.
Meanwhile, some AI-related names showed a sluggish rebound. Kioxia Holdings (285A.T) and SoftBank Group (9984.T) moved weakly.

sum: Asian technology stocks suffered steep losses on Friday as investors extended a sell-off in global equities, with concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence investment and the potential for tighter US restrictions on data center construction hitting semiconductor manufacturers and technology investors.

South Korean chipmakers led the regional decline. SK Hynix plunged 10.44%, while Samsung Electronics fell 6.35%. LG Innotek lost 7.02%, and LG Display declined 4.45%, as investors reduced exposure to companies closely linked to the global technology supply chain.

The selling also spread across Japan, where semiconductor equipment manufacturers and companies with significant AI investment exposure came under pressure. Advantest, which makes chip-testing equipment, dropped 4.99%, while Tokyo Electron fell more than 5%. SoftBank Group, a major technology investor, tumbled 10.83%.

sum: The Nikkei 225 began trading higher on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on November 5, opening at 62,384.73 yen, up 196.10 yen (0.32%) from the previous trading day. Buying led the market, carrying over the momentum from gains in all three major U.S. stock indexes the prior day.

Two factors pushed the market up. One was the firm performance of the U.S. stock market as it digested the results of the U.S. midterm elections. The other was a sharp drop in crude oil prices as views spread that tensions in the Middle East were easing. Lower energy costs support investor sentiment through both corporate earnings and household burdens.
Among blue-chip shares, Toyota Motor (7203.T) surged, while Sony Group (6758.T) and index-heavyweight Fast Retailing (9983.T) were quoted higher.

On the other hand, artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor-related shares saw notable declines. SoftBank Group (9984.T), Tokyo Electron (8035.T), and Advantest (6857.T) all fell sharply, as caution over the direction of AI regulation continued to simmer.

In the previous day's trading on November 4, these three semiconductor and AI-related stocks alone pushed the Nikkei 225 down by about 1,241 yen at one point. Selling tends to concentrate in stocks with large index weightings, and this structure continues to amplify swings across the broader market.

Among market participants, the near-term focus is whether buybacks will emerge in the sharply fallen semiconductor shares. On the previous day, some stocks such as Fast Retailing and Nintendo (7974.T) rose, so the market was not uniformly lower. Some see the fact that buying interest is not one-sided as a sign of the market's underlying resilience.

On the overseas front, reports on vote counting in the U.S. midterm elections were also coming in during Tokyo trading hours, and market participants are focused on how U.S. long-term interest rates and foreign exchange rates react. Domestically, earnings announcements from companies such as IHI (7013.T), Mitsubishi Corp (8058.T), and NTT (9432.T) are scheduled during trading hours, and stock price reactions to individual earnings results could divide winners and losers within sectors.

Tokyo Shares Tumble Wednesday Despite Strong Corporate Earnings
sum: TOKYO - Japan's Nikkei 225 Stock Average closed at 62,188.63 on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, falling 893.23 points, or 1.42%, from the previous trading session as heavy selling in semiconductor and artificial intelligence-related stocks swept through Tokyo markets following the U.S. midterm elections, although a strong afternoon recovery helped the benchmark recover much of its earlier losses.

The Nikkei suffered its third consecutive decline after trading resumed following the November 3 Culture Day holiday. The benchmark opened at 62,973.16, briefly moved into positive territory, and then plunged as investors reduced exposure to technology stocks and other companies vulnerable to changes in U.S. economic and regulatory policies. By the 11:30 a.m. morning close, the index had fallen 2,246.50 points, or 3.56%, to 60,835.36, while the broader TOPIX index dropped 98.01 points to 3,832.27.

Selling intensified during the early afternoon, with the Nikkei approaching the psychologically important 60,000-point level before bargain hunters entered the market. The recovery gathered momentum later in the session, reducing the benchmark's losses to 1,206 points by 3 p.m. and continuing into the close.

Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest was among the largest contributors to the decline, alongside Tokyo Electron, SoftBank Group, Kioxia Holdings and Kyocera. Investors were concerned that increased scrutiny of major technology companies and tighter regulations on artificial intelligence following the U.S. elections could affect spending on data centers and advanced semiconductors. Selling also reflected unease over high valuations following the substantial gains recorded by technology shares earlier in the year.

Other technology and industrial companies, including Sumitomo Electric Industries, Furukawa Electric, Taiyo Yuden and Murata Manufacturing, came under pressure. Nonferrous metals, petroleum and coal products, mining and electrical equipment were among the weakest sectors, while airlines, real estate companies and railway operators attracted selective buying.
Fast Retailing, the operator of Uniqlo, provided support for the Nikkei, while Nintendo and Yamato Holdings also attracted buyers.

Tokyo Electron stock jumps 6%; AI forecast needs ¥662B H2 profit
sum: Tokyo Electron shares rose 6.3% to ¥10,115 in Tokyo at 10:19 a.m. JST on Monday, November 2, according to a Yahoo Finance Japan exchange quote. Friday's close was ¥9,514. The move follows the chip-equipment maker's October 30 forecast for ¥1.169 trillion in operating profit in the fiscal year ending March 2027, up 87.1% from the preceding year. The forecast itself is three days old; Monday's share-price response is the new development.

The stock's more demanding test is in the second half of that fiscal year. Tokyo Electron's earnings release puts first-half operating profit at ¥506.8 billion and full-year profit at ¥1.169 trillion. Subtracting the first half leaves ¥662.2 billion for October through March, about 30.7% more than the first half. The company shows the same second-half estimate in its presentation, but the comparison is the point investors should carry into a forecast: the guidance needs another step up after an unusually strong first half.

There is a second, less obvious number in the October 30 documents. Tokyo Electron authorized a repurchase facility with separate limits of 25 million shares and ¥150 billion. At the observed ¥10,115 price, buying all 25 million shares would cost about ¥252.9 billion. The cash limit would instead cover about 14.8 million shares, or 0.65% of the 2.2698 billion shares outstanding excluding treasury stock cited in the notice. This is a price-based sensitivity, not a claim that the company bought any shares. The often quoted 1.1% share ceiling cannot be treated as an automatic reduction at Monday's price.

The ¥10,115 observation is a fixed publication snapshot, not a continuously updated price. Yahoo's underlying one-minute chart marked its last trade at 10:19:52 a.m. JST; it was about 15 minutes old when checked at 10:35 a.m. JST. The Tokyo Stock Exchange was in its morning session. At that quoted price, the stock was ¥601 above the October 30 close, or 6.32% using ¥9,514 as the denominator. A later trade can change the move without changing what this timestamped observation records.

sum: In the Tokyo stock market on the 28th, the Nikkei Stock Average opened higher and extended its gains. It opened at 63,738.98, up 470.61 points from the previous trading day. Carrying over the momentum from the prior day's U.S. market, where tech stocks led buying, funds flowed into artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor-related names. The advance briefly exceeded 900 points, and the morning session closed at 64,067.10, up 798.73 points.

Driving the market higher were high-priced semiconductor stocks with large weightings in the index. Advantest (6857.T), Tokyo Electron (8035.T), and SoftBank Group (9984.T) together lifted the Nikkei by roughly 450 points. Among individual names, Hitachi (6501.T) and Toyota Motor (7203.T) were also firm. On the other hand, financial and value stocks such as Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (8316.T) and Sony Group (6758.T) got off to a soft start.

The breadth of buying was limited. The Tokyo Stock Price Index (TOPIX) moved in the opposite direction, down 0.84 points at 3,996.53 at the morning close, and more than half of Prime Market issues declined. The buying was concentrated in a handful of large-cap tech stocks that drive the index, and some market participants said they want to "see the actual earnings results" before interim corporate earnings announcements get into full swing.

Behind the move is a rally in U.S. tech stocks. Expectations for semiconductor-related shares grew stronger as U.S. AI developer Anthropic is increasingly expected to proceed with an initial public offering (IPO). With tech stocks rising in the prior day's U.S. market, related names led buying in Tokyo as well.

In trading on the 29th, the advance widened further, with the Nikkei at one point rising to 64,773.69, up 819.50 points from the previous day. Interest in companies posting strong earnings, such as Advantest, remained strong, and the index is testing whether it can hold at elevated levels.

Investor attention is shifting to whether the semiconductor stocks that have lifted the index can sustain their gains after the earnings announcements. If the concentration in high-priced stocks continues, risks remain that the market as a whole will lack firmness, as suggested by TOPIX's sluggishness and the declines among Prime Market issues.

Nikkei CNBC-style market commentary would likely focus on the powerful but narrow nature of the rally. The headline index looked strong because AI and semiconductor stocks rose sharply, but the broader market was far less convincing.

The broader TOPIX was much less buoyant, showing that the rally was concentrated in high-priced Nikkei components and technology shares. The contrast suggested that investors were not buying the whole market evenly, but were instead returning to the AI and semiconductor names that had been under pressure earlier in the week.

Advantest was the largest positive contributor to the Nikkei during midday trading, reflecting renewed buying in chip-testing shares. The company remains one of Japan’s most direct beneficiaries of demand for advanced AI processors and high-performance computing.

Analysts note that technology and growth-focused companies, which are expected to generate high earnings in the future, are particularly vulnerable in such an environment.

sum: Teradyne TER and Applied Materials AMAT are major players in the semiconductor market. While Teradyne focuses on semiconductor test equipment and automation solutions, Applied Materials specializes in semiconductor manufacturing equipment used to fabricate advanced chips.
So, TER or AMAT — Which of these Semiconductor stocks has the greater upside potential? Let's find out.

Teradyne is benefiting from the growing demand for AI infrastructure, which is driving robust growth across its semiconductor test and robotics divisions. Growth is largely attributed to the accelerating demand for AI and data center technologies, with AI-related demand accounting for nearly 70% of Teradyne's revenues in the first quarter of 2026, up from about 60% in the previous quarter.

The company's product innovation is supporting its growth. Teradyne's introduction, like the Photon 100 platform for silicon photonics and co-packaged optics testing and the Omnyx production board test platform, addresses critical needs in AI data center build-outs. The Photon 100 is expected to contribute to a TAM expansion opportunity that could reach $300 million to $700 million per year over the midterm.

Teradyne's expanding portfolio has been noteworthy. The company recently announced a known good device screening test cell solution. This solution was developed in partnership with Tokyo Electron (TEL) for AI and data center semiconductor applications. It combines Teradyne's UltraFLEXplus test platform with TEL's Prexa SDP prober. This combination allows for high-quality device screening across advanced packaging flows.

The solution is designed for chiplet-based 2.5D and 3D architectures. It helps improve yield, boost reliability, and lower integration risks in high-volume manufacturing. Its open ecosystem architecture provides flexibility for integration with various probe cards, manipulators and interface technologies.

Applied Materials is emerging as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI-driven semiconductor investment cycle. The company is seeing AI adoption broaden and diversify, which is pushing wafer fab equipment spending toward leading-edge foundry-logic, DRAM and advanced packaging.

sum: As the global semiconductor industry seeks paths beyond Moore's Law, advanced packaging has emerged as a critical avenue for boosting chip performance. sum: High-bandwidth memory (HBM) now accounts for about 15% of total DRAM production, reflecting rapidly rising demand for the technology. Continued investment in advanced packaging, including HBM, is also expected to drive strong growth in the semiconductor equipment market this year.

Bryce Hill, chief financial officer of Applied Materials, said at the Cantor Fitzgerald Global Technology Industry Growth Conference on March 10 that about 15% of DRAM wafers are now allocated to HBM production. "The market is being driven by strong demand for memory semiconductors," he said.

The remark suggests that memory manufacturers including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology are dedicating roughly 15% of their DRAM production capacity to HBM. According to data from market research firm TrendForce, HBM accounted for only about 1.5% of the overall DRAM market as of March 2023. Its share has increased roughly tenfold in three years.

Growth in the data-center sector is currently the main driver of memory demand. Data centers now account for about 30% of total wafer demand, overtaking PCs to become the second-largest segment in the market. Starting next year, the amount of memory included in graphics processing unit (GPU) systems is expected to increase by about 33% compared with current levels. By 2029, the segment is expected to surpass smartphones, which currently represent the largest share of memory demand.

The expanding HBM market is expected to significantly boost revenue for related semiconductor equipment makers. Hill said equipment for leading-edge logic and packaging is likely to grow faster than the broader semiconductor equipment market, which is expected to expand about 20% this year. "Investment related to HBM will continue, leading to rapid growth," he said.

Applied Materials also noted that producing HBM with the same capacity as conventional DRAM requires about three times more wafer area. The structure and manufacturing process are more complex than those for standard DRAM products. As a result, memory manufacturers must use more wafers to supply customers with the same capacity as conventional DRAM, which in turn increases demand for manufacturing equipment.

items.t: Micron's Valuation Puzzle: Record Earnings, Contract Backlog, and a Market That Refuses to Look Up
sum: The disconnect playing out in Micron Technology's stock is becoming one of the more striking anomalies in the semiconductor space. The memory chip maker just posted the strongest gross margin in its history — 84.9 percent — and quarterly revenue that nearly quadrupled year over year. Yet the share price closed Monday at 691.20 euros, down 3.29 percent on the session and roughly 37 percent below the 52-week high of 1,103.80 euros reached in late June.

That gap between operational excellence and market performance has analysts wrestling with a central question: Is this a valuation reset for a company whose fundamentals remain intact, or the first sign that the memory cycle is turning sooner than expected?

The recent selling pressure traces back to early August, when South Korean memory rivals Samsung and SK Hynix suffered sharp declines after an extended run of retail speculation. The pullback rippled across the entire semiconductor complex — what market participants describe as a "leverage washout" — dragging Micron down with it despite no change in the company's underlying business.

The broader context is equally turbulent. Since late July, memory and AI-related names have been under siege. Western Digital, Applied Materials, Marvell, AMD, and Nvidia all slid in tandem at various points, fueled by skepticism about AI valuations and weak preliminary results from Samsung. Reports that Chinese firm DeepSeek is developing its own AI chip — reducing China's reliance on Nvidia and Huawei — added to the anxiety. In Japan, Tokyo Electron lost nearly 11 percent in a single session while memory maker Kioxia tumbled more than 18 percent.

A strategist at Standard Chartered pointed to media coverage of China's ambitions in memory chips and lithography equipment as a key driver of the negative sentiment. Add to that analyst projections suggesting memory chip prices could peak as early as 2027, and the bear case begins to take shape.

While the stock stumbles, the business is firing on all cylinders. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, which ended May 28, Micron generated record revenue of 41.4 billion dollars — a 346 percent jump from the prior-year period. Earnings per share came in at 24.67 dollars, up 1,368 percent, with growth across all four business segments.

Consensus expectations are tightly clustered around management’s prior guidance, with EPS estimates ranging only $0.10 from low to high and revenue estimates spanning just $170M. The 28.6% year-over-year EPS growth rate represents an acceleration from the 3.4% growth recorded in the same quarter last year, consistent with the industry’s ongoing recovery from the 2022-2023 downcycle.

The more consequential debate centers on gross margin. Management’s guided midpoint of 48.5% represents a 180-basis-point decline from the prior quarter’s 50.3%, a step-down that management attributed to product and geographic mix shifts rather than pricing pressure or cost inflation. SoftBank shares plunge nearly 9%, extending selloff into third day
sum: Shares of SoftBank Group plunged nearly 9% on Friday, marking its third straight day of selloff after the Japanese giant said it had sold its entire stake in U.S. chip giant Nvidia for $5.83 billion.

The stock pared losses to trade 6.57% lower as of 3 a.m. ET, marking the second straight week of selloff after the conglomerate saw almost $50 billion in market cap wiped out last week — its worst weekly loss since March 2020.

"The sell-off of SoftBank today is less idiosyncratic to SoftBank, and more driven by broader market sentiment on semiconductors and technology stocks," said Rolf Bulk, a senior equity analyst at New Street Research.
"In that context and with SoftBank's holding discount still very low vs. historic averages, SoftBank trading down 5-6% today does not surprise me."
SoftBank disclosed in its latest earnings that it offloaded 32.1 million Nvidia shares in October and scaled back its T-Mobile stake, bringing in $9.17 billion.

Although the Nvidia sale surprised some investors, it isn't the first time SoftBank has exited the U.S. chip giant. Its Vision Fund had accumulated roughly $4 billion worth of Nvidia shares in 2017 before selling out entirely in early 2019.

Even so, SoftBank continues to have business ties to Nvidia. The Tokyo-based company is involved in a number of AI ventures that use Nvidia's technology, including the $500 billion Stargate project for data centers in the U.S.

items.t: Will the Nikkei 225 sustain its momentum into 2026?
sum: In the short term, asymmetric downside risk warrants more conservative stop losses in trading setups
[SINGAPORE] The Nikkei 225 Index Futures, traded in standard, mini, and micro contracts, is a derivative instrument based on Japan’s flagship equity benchmark, the Nikkei 225 Index.
The top three constituents by weight are Advantest (semiconductor testing solutions), Softbank (multinational investment holding company), and Fast Retailing (Uniqlo).

As of Nov 5, 14:30 SGT, the Nikkei 225 stood at 50,212, down 2.50 per cent on the day but still up +25.86 per cent year to date in JPY terms after a strong +16.63 per cent rally in October. The sell-off was likely driven by an overnight slump in US Tech, with AMD’s mixed earnings report weighing on investor sentiment across global semiconductor names.

Adding to the cautious tone, several Wall Street CEOs, including Morgan Stanley’s Ted Pick and Goldman Sachs’ David Solomon, warned of a possible equity drawdown of more than 10 per cent in the next 10 to 12 months, while Capital Group’s Mike Gitlin mentioned stretched valuations despite strong corporate earnings.

Furthermore, Michael Burry, the fund manager known for The Big Short, disclosed bearish puts on Palantir and Nvidia In post-market trading. The Nikkei 225’s heavier tech weighting (~55 per cent versus the S&P 500’s 36 per cent) exacerbated the decline, with semiconductor firms like Tokyo Electron and Advantest leading losses.
Nevertheless, absent a sustained drawdown, we expect the Nikkei 225 to maintain its uptrend towards the end of the year.
